about: Consolidation, Integration and Feedback Week A (MBBS0020) is a 0-credit Term 1 week in UCL's MBBS Year 1, the first of three such weeks. UCL's module page says it is timetabled in November and is designed to consolidate and integrate the preceding modules, with formative assessment and feedback. UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 assessment guide says the November and February CIF weeks include online formative papers combining knowledge and practical content, using five-option SBA and VSA (no more than five words) questions, the same types used in the summative Applied Knowledge Tests. This guide explains the week and how to prepare; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What CIF Week A is and where it fits
notes.body:
Consolidation, Integration and Feedback Week A (MBBS0020) is not a taught subject with its own syllabus. It is a review week in Term 1 of UCL's MBBS Year 1, and UCL's module catalogue describes it as the first of three such weeks.

What the official module page says
- Its purpose is to consolidate and integrate the modules that come before it and to give you formative assessment and feedback.
- It is timetabled in November, taught in person, and carries 0 credits.
- It is open only to students on the MBBS programme.

Where it sits in the year
- Year 1 opens with an introduction and orientation period, followed by Foundations of Health and Medical Practice and then Infection and Defence. In the 2025–26 timetable, CIF A fell in late November, straight after Infection and Defence and before Circulation and Breathing began. Check your own year's timetable, as dates move.
- There are two more weeks of the same kind later in the year: CIF B (Term 2) and CIF C (Term 3), each after a later block of teaching.
- An older UCL Year 1 study guide (2018–19) described the CIF weeks as a mix of revision, case-based and lecture-theatre sessions that link the preceding module with the other strands of the course, followed by formative assessment and feedback. Treat that as background only; the current arrangements are on the Year 1 Moodle pages.

Why it matters even though it is formative
- Formative means the mark does not count towards progression. The paper is designed to show you the question types used in the summative Applied Knowledge Tests at the end of the year, and to show you, early, which topics you have not yet secured.
- Because the week integrates material, expect questions that cross module boundaries. For example, a clinical scenario about an infection may also test anatomy, pharmacology principles or communication.

Exam tips: treat CIF A as a dress rehearsal. Sit the paper honestly without notes so the feedback reflects what you actually know.

notes.h: The online formative paper: SBA and VSA questions
notes.body:
UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments document says the CIF weeks (November and February) include online integrated formative assessments that combine knowledge and practical testing in a single paper. The February one is a mock run under exam conditions. Two question formats are used, the same ones as in the summative Applied Knowledge Tests (AKTs).

Single Best Answer (SBA)
- A clinical or scientific stem, a lead-in question, and five options. Several options may be partly right; you must choose the best one.
- Technique: read the lead-in first so you know what is being asked (diagnosis? mechanism? next step?). Then read the stem and try to answer before looking at the options ("cover the options"). Eliminate options that are wrong or less specific.
- Watch for qualifiers such as "most likely", "first", "most appropriate", and for laboratory values or images that change the answer.

Very Short Answer (VSA)
- You type your own answer of no more than five words, so you cannot recognise the answer from a list. This tests genuine recall.
- Technique: give the specific term asked for (for example the name of a cell, organism, nerve or structure) and spell it accurately. Do not hedge with two answers.
- Practise by covering the options of SBA questions and answering as a VSA.

Practical content
- Practical knowledge (for example anatomy, histology or data interpretation) is tested inside the same online paper, so images may appear in either question type.

The summative AKTs, for context
- The 2026–27 document describes two AKT papers at the end of Year 1, each two hours long, online, worth up to 100 marks, mixing SBA and VSA questions that may include images, with no negative marking. Because there is no negative marking, you should always answer every question.

Exam tips: time yourself. Two hours for up to 100 marks is a little over a minute per mark, so practise moving on from a hard SBA and returning to it.

notes.h: Using your feedback and preparing for the week
notes.body:
The value of CIF A lies in what you do with the results. The week is designed to give you formative feedback on your progress.

Before the week: how to prepare
- Revise Foundations of Health and Medical Practice and Infection and Defence actively: self-testing with question banks, flashcards and explaining topics aloud work better than rereading.
- Use the learning objectives and resources on the Year 1 Moodle pages as your checklist; the formative paper is written to the teaching you have had.
- Integrate as you revise: for each topic, ask how it links to anatomy and histology, to the clinical and professional practice strands, and to communication and ethics.
- Do a few timed blocks of SBA questions and some recall practice in VSA style, so the format is not new on the day.

After the paper: using the feedback
- Go through every question you got wrong and also every one you guessed correctly. Classify each error: knowledge gap, misread question, poor technique (for example not reading the lead-in), or running out of time.
- Make a short action list of topics to relearn, and schedule them into your revision before the next block's teaching takes over.
- Revisit missed topics after a gap (spaced repetition) rather than once immediately.
- If your performance worries you, talk to your personal tutor. UCL also has student support and well-being services for problems that are affecting your study.

Looking ahead
- CIF B (February) is described as a mock under exam conditions and, according to the older study guide, covers all modules to date, not just the latest one. Keep earlier material alive with regular spaced review.

Exam tips: the main point of a formative paper is to find your gaps. A low score with a clear action plan is more useful than a high score you cannot explain.

notes.h: Practice questions in the SBA and VSA styles
notes.body:
The questions in this section are practice in UCL's formats (five-option SBA, and short recall answers like VSAs) on standard basic-science content of the kind covered in the first Year 1 modules. They are not taken from UCL papers, and UCL's module pages do not list the exact content of the CIF A paper, so use the Moodle learning objectives to check coverage.

How to use them
- Answer each SBA before looking at the options, then check your answer against the options.
- For each VSA-style item, write no more than five words and check your spelling.
- Read the explanations even when you are right: they show why the other options are wrong, which is how distractors are built in real papers.

Core ideas these questions draw on
- Antibody-producing cells and antibody classes: plasma cells (differentiated B cells) secrete antibody; IgM is the first class made in a primary response; IgG is the main class in secondary responses and the only one to cross the placenta.
- Antigen presentation: dendritic cells are the most effective at activating naive T cells; helper T cells carry CD4 and recognise antigen on MHC class II, while cytotoxic T cells carry CD8 and recognise MHC class I.
- Bacterial structure: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains crystal violet (purple); Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide, and stain pink with the counterstain.
- Innate immunity: neutrophils are the first cells recruited in large numbers to acute bacterial infection.

Exam tips: build your own bank as you revise. Turn each learning objective into one SBA (five options, one best answer) and one VSA, then swap with a friend.

questions.q: A 19-year-old has a confirmed bacterial infection. Blood tests some days later show rising specific antibody. Which cell type is directly secreting this antibody?
questions.why: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B-lymphocytes specialised for secreting antibody. Naive B-lymphocytes carry antibody on their surface but do not secrete it in quantity; helper T cells support B-lymphocyte activation; macrophages and dendritic cells phagocytose and present antigen but do not make antibody.

questions.q: A Gram stain of a bacterium shows pink rods. Which structural feature best explains this result?
options: Thin peptidoglycan layer with an outer membrane
Mycolic acids in the cell wall
questions.why: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane; the alcohol wash removes crystal violet and they take up the pink counterstain. A thick wall retains crystal violet (purple); bacteria without a wall or with mycolic acids stain poorly; a capsule does not determine the Gram reaction.

questions.q: Which cell is most effective at activating naive T lymphocytes in a lymph node?
questions.why: Dendritic cells capture antigen in tissues, migrate to lymph nodes and present it with co-stimulatory signals to naive T cells. Neutrophils, mast cells and eosinophils are innate effector cells, and plasma cells secrete antibody.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a Single Best Answer (SBA) and a Very Short Answer (VSA) question as used in UCL's Year 1 papers, and give one technique for answering each.
markScheme: SBA: stem and lead-in with five options; choose the single best answer (others may be partly correct)
VSA: candidate types own answer of no more than five words; tests recall without cues
SBA technique: read the lead-in first / answer before looking at options / eliminate weaker options
VSA technique: give one specific, correctly spelled term; do not offer alternatives
questions.modelAnswer: An SBA question gives a clinical or scientific stem, a lead-in and five options, several of which may be partly true; the task is to pick the single best answer. A VSA question gives no options: you type your own answer of no more than five words, so it tests recall rather than recognition. For SBAs, read the lead-in first and try to answer before looking at the options, then eliminate options that are wrong or less specific. For VSAs, give one precise term, spelled correctly, rather than hedging with several possibilities.

questions.q: VSA practice (no more than five words each): (a) Name the antibody class produced first in a primary immune response. (b) Name the surface marker that defines helper T cells.
